title: Honey on the letters
hookLine: a medieval custom: children licked honey from letters on their first day of learning

cards: A small slate, with the Hebrew alphabet written across it: alef, bet, gimel, all the way through. Someone has spread honey over every letter.

A boy, small enough that he was carried in, sits in front of it beside his teacher. The teacher points to the first letter and says its name, and the boy repeats it. Then the teacher tells him to lick the honey off.
He does. Next letter, next lick. His face is sticky, he's grinning, and the grown-ups in the doorway are grinning too.
That's how the custom pictures a child's very first day of learning.

teach.b: An old custom for a child's first day of Torah study. First, how it went. In the versions old Jewish books describe, a child was wrapped in a prayer shawl and carried to the teacher, so that even the walk felt set apart.
Letters were written on a slate and covered in honey to lick off, and some versions add cakes and eggs with verses written on them, eaten after the lesson. Details vary from telling to telling.
The heart doesn't: the first taste of learning is sweet. Second, the prophet who ate a scroll. In Ezekiel, the prophet is handed a scroll and told to eat it.
He does, and he says: "it was in my mouth as honey for sweetness." Words, taken in so completely they become food, and they taste of honey. Third, the Psalms.
Psalm nineteen calls God's teachings more precious than gold and sweeter than honey from the comb.

teach.h: A SCROLL THAT TASTED OF HONEY.
teach.b: The custom takes that line at its word: start with honey, and let the child find out the rest is sweeter still.

teach.h: A DROP ON A LETTER CARD.
teach.b: Some Jewish schools and families still put a drop of honey on a letter card when a child begins to read Hebrew. A grown-up doesn't need a slate.
But the question carries: what would it take for the next thing you learn to taste sweet, not like a chore?

how: Some Jewish schools and families mark a child's first Hebrew lesson by putting honey on letters for the child to taste, echoing an old custom for the first day of Torah study.

games.why: letter by letter, the child repeats and tastes, so the first memory of learning is sweet.

practice: If you have honey or anything sweet, put a little on your fingertip or your tongue; if you don't, imagine it.
Then read one line you'd like to learn, a verse, a poem, a sentence from a book on your shelf, slowly, once, while the sweetness is still there.
Close your eyes and say it back, and if it slips, read it again, letting the taste and the words arrive together.

wordCard.voice: Honey on the letters. A child's first lesson, licked off a slate, because the words were meant to taste sweet from the start. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: learning is sweet. Honey first, and then the letters, one by one. See you tomorrow.
